I ran a website that got 100K visits/month in the gaming space, and can tell you that AdBlock usage is just too high to rely on traditional display advertising. It was a full 50% of users and rising steadily. A freemium type of model, like Reddit Gold is, feels like a much better solution. People that pay get a little something extra, and everyone gets a good experience that isn't filled with ads.

It's unfortunate. Advertisers pretty much shot themselves in the head with pop-ups starting in the early 2000s, and the continual war to try to force them on you in one way or another has ultimately ended up with webmasters throwing hissy fits because they didn't want users to stop accepting ads just because of the virus someone caught on their computer from an ad on their site and because the ads dominated user screens with usually-deceptive ads. Accordingly, users just dumped on more and more anti-ad software because they wanted their computer to be safe, didn't want a screenful of ads yelling at them that they'd "won" something, and got tired of grandma calling to say that her computer was "broadcasting its IP to the KGB" because of a fake anti-virus window.

I'm sure there were much more legitimate advertising agencies out there, but I'd be surprised if they aren't out of business by now.
Maybe Google text ads would be the best solution as adblockers can allow them, as they are unobtrusive and they can generate revenue without being in-your-face

Unpopular opinion time:

Charging a small monthly fee. Don't get me wrong, I like free stuff, but it would stop (or make difficult) sock puppet accounts and novelty accounts. I'm only talking a couple of dollars a month. It would also cover the hosting fees.

The other alternatives have already been shown to us through Digg and then Reddit. The site continues to grow and grow until some billionaire wants to make some real money - original owners realise that they can't turn a profit so let the billionaires take over. They sanitize and ruin the site (while trying to pander to an audience of dullards), sending it spiralling into a shadow of its former self and the interesting user base moves on.

If we don't want Voat to become another Digg or Reddit or MySpace, then we might have to pay for it.
